passage: "So people think I'm restless. And fine, I am, a bit. My name's Vidya, I'm sixteen, and there's always a pen cap in my mouth. I tap my foot through every class. To study I need loud music, really loud, or my brain won't sit still. My best friend Nilesh is the opposite. At the school fest he wore ear defenders and ate only the plain parathas he brought from home. Some people laughed. But he knows himself. That's what we worked out together. We both have bodies that react strongly, just in different directions. So I carry a chewy bracelet instead of wrecking pens, and I ask to sit at the back so my tapping doesn't bother anyone. Nilesh plans his quiet corner before every event. It's not weird. It's a plan."

qa.q: What did Nilesh bring from home to the school fest?
qa.a: Plain parathas, and he wore ear defenders.

qa.q: How does Vidya seem to feel about being called restless?
qa.a: Vidya accepts it without shame and seems proud that Vidya and Nilesh understand themselves well enough to plan.

qa.q: What choices does Vidya make to manage the need for movement?
qa.a: Vidya carries a chewy bracelet instead of chewing pens and sits at the back so the tapping doesn't bother anyone.

qa.q: How might the people who laughed at Nilesh see him if they heard Vidya?
qa.a: They might see him as someone who knows what his body needs and plans for it, not as someone strange.

grounding: It shows a teenager who chews, fidgets and craves loud music and a friend who covers his ears and avoids foods, both using self-knowledge to plan.

passage: My brother Omkar is fifteen, and at our cousin's wedding I watched him closely. I can't say what was in his head, only what I saw. When the band started, he pressed both hands over his ears and stepped behind a pillar. At dinner he took only curd rice and left the fried items untouched. But he wasn't sulking. Before we went, he had asked Mummy which hall had the quiet garden, and he'd packed earplugs in his pocket. When the dancing began, he nodded to me and went out to that garden. Later he came back in for the photos, smiling properly. "I just needed ten minutes," he told me. "I know how much noise I can take." I'm Neelam, by the way. I used to call him boring. I don't now.

qa.q: What did Omkar take at dinner?
qa.a: Only curd rice.

qa.q: What does Omkar's line 'I know how much noise I can take' suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he understands his own needs and feels confident planning around them.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's choices helped him enjoy the wedding?
qa.a: He asked about the quiet garden in advance, carried earplugs and took a short break before the photos.

qa.q: How has Neelam's view of Omkar changed?
qa.a: Neelam used to call him boring, but now sees that he is managing the noise wisely.

grounding: A sibling watches a teenager who covers his ears in a crowd and avoids certain foods, and sees how his self-knowledge lets him plan.

passage: In their Chennai flat, Shankar, fifteen, did homework with music thumping in his headphones, one leg bouncing, a pen cap chewed flat between his teeth. His younger brother Darshan, fourteen, sat at the other end of the table with foam plugs in his ears and a biscuit he had checked for crunchiness. Amma used to say they were opposites. Last month the school nurse had helped them each make a list of what calms them. Now Shankar kept a rubber chew band in his pocket for exams. And when the family planned the temple festival on Saturday, Darshan said, "I'll come at six, before the crowd, with my earmuffs." Shankar said, "I'll come at eight, when the drums start." Amma laughed and agreed.

qa.q: What was Shankar chewing while doing homework?
qa.a: He was chewing a pen cap flat between his teeth.

qa.q: How did Darshan seem to feel about crowds and noise?
qa.a: He seemed uneasy and easily overwhelmed by them, using earplugs at home and planning to arrive before the crowd with earmuffs.

qa.q: How did knowing themselves help the brothers plan the festival?
qa.a: Each chose a time and tool that suited his needs: Darshan came early with earmuffs, Shankar came when the drums started.

qa.q: How does Amma see her two sons' differences now?
qa.a: She sees them as opposites but accepts both, laughing and agreeing to their separate plans.

grounding: Shows one teenager who chews, fidgets and wants loud music, and another who avoids noise and certain foods, both using self-knowledge to plan.

passage:
"Siami, the fest plan. You're on the stage crew with me, right?" Vasudha drummed on the desk.
"Near the speakers? No way, Vasu. Last year I had to leave after ten minutes."
"But the music is the best part! I need it loud. It's like it wakes my whole body up."
"And for me it's like being hit." Lalremsiami pressed her fingers to her ears just thinking about it. "I'll take the craft stall at the back. It's quiet there."
"Okay. But we meet at the gate at six for noodles."
"Six. And I'm bringing my earplugs for the walk past the stage."
"Deal. I'll bring gum. I chew it all day on fest days."
"I know," Siami laughed. "You chewed through three packs last year."

qa.q: Where will Lalremsiami work during the fest?
qa.a: She will take the craft stall at the back, where it is quiet.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami feel about loud music near the speakers?
qa.a: She feels overwhelmed and distressed by it, describing it as being hit and covering her ears just thinking about it.

qa.q: What makes their plan work for both of them?
qa.a: Each chose a spot and tools that fit their own needs, and they set a meeting time at the gate so they still share the evening.

qa.q: How does Vasudha experience the loud music differently?
qa.a: For Vasudha it is energising, like it wakes the whole body up, which is why Vasudha wants to be near the speakers.

grounding: Shows one teenager who craves loud music and chewing, and another who avoids noise, both knowing themselves well enough to plan.

passage: I'm Suraj, and at sixteen I thought I was just a restless kid. I bounced my knee in every class, chewed my hoodie strings, needed to slam a football against the wall before I could study. Teachers told me to sit still. My friend Bidisha was the opposite. She hated the canteen noise, wouldn't eat anything slimy, and covered her ears at assemblies. We used to joke we were two broken radios. Then in Class 11 our biology teacher explained that some bodies seek more input and some avoid it. That made sense to me. I started doing push-ups before exams and keeping a stress ball in my pocket. Bidisha started eating lunch in the courtyard. We weren't broken. We were just learning how to tune ourselves.

qa.q: What did Suraj need to do before studying?
qa.a: Suraj needed to slam a football against the wall.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel about the restlessness before Class 11?
qa.a: Suraj felt misunderstood and a bit ashamed, being told to sit still and joking about being a broken radio.

qa.q: How did self-knowledge change things for Suraj?
qa.a: Understanding the need for input led Suraj to plan push-ups before exams and carry a stress ball.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel after starting to eat in the courtyard?
qa.a: Bidisha may feel calmer and more comfortable, away from the canteen noise that bothered her.

grounding: Shows one teenager who seeks input by moving and chewing and another who avoids noise and textures, both learning to plan with self-knowledge.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10 science trip.
Yusuf chewed through two pencil caps on the bus and asked to play loud music on his headphones. At the museum he kept tapping the railings. When I gave him a squeeze ball, he calmed a lot and asked good questions about the rockets.
Nandini, in the same group, covered her ears in the crowded dome and wouldn't eat the canteen food. She seemed anxious, and her hands were shaking.
Afterwards I met them one by one. Yusuf now keeps a fidget and chewing gum in his bag for long days. Nandini made a card: step out when crowds get loud, bring her own lunch. Both said it helped to know their bodies weren't "being weird," just asking for different things.

qa.q: What did the counsellor give Yusuf at the museum?
qa.a: A squeeze ball.

qa.q: How did Yusuf seem to feel before he got the squeeze ball?
qa.a: He seemed restless and unsettled, chewing, tapping and wanting loud music, and was calmer once his body had something to do.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do next, and why was it useful?
qa.a: The counsellor met each student to plan: Yusuf keeps a fidget and gum, Nandini steps out of loud crowds and brings lunch, so both can manage their needs with self-knowledge.

qa.q: How might the trip have felt for Nandini?
qa.a: The crowded dome probably felt overwhelming and scary for her, with covered ears and shaking hands.

grounding: A counsellor notes one teenager seeking input by chewing and fidgeting and another avoiding crowds and foods, and helps both plan with self-knowledge.
